The Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem gives a useful way to interpret a coefficient
in a multiple regression. It also provides a practical check on an estimation
workflow.

Suppose the regression is

$$
Y = \alpha + \beta D + X'\gamma + U,
$$

where $D$ is the regressor of interest and $X$ contains the controls. The
coefficient $\widehat\beta$ is unchanged if we:

1. regress $Y$ on $X$ and retain the residuals;
2. regress $D$ on $X$ and retain the residuals; and
3. regress the residualized outcome on the residualized regressor.

The result follows because residualization projects both variables onto the
space orthogonal to the controls. The final regression compares only the
variation in $Y$ and $D$ that the controls do not explain.

## Verify the result in R

The example uses only base R. We generate an outcome in which treatment and a
control are correlated, then compare the treatment coefficient from the full
regression with the coefficient from the residual regression.

```{r}
#| label: fwl-simulation

set.seed(20260811)
n <- 1000

x <- rnorm(n)
d <- 0.8 * x + rnorm(n)
y <- 1 + 2 * d - 0.5 * x + rnorm(n)

full_model <- lm(y ~ d + x)
y_residual <- resid(lm(y ~ x))
d_residual <- resid(lm(d ~ x))
partial_model <- lm(y_residual ~ d_residual)

coefficients <- c(
  full_regression = unname(coef(full_model)["d"]),
  partial_regression = unname(coef(partial_model)["d_residual"])
)

print(round(coefficients, 10))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(coefficients[[1]], coefficients[[2]])))
```

The two estimates are equal up to numerical precision. This identity is
algebraic: it does not require the regression to have a causal interpretation.
A causal interpretation of $\widehat\beta$ still requires assumptions that
make the residual variation in $D$ conditionally exogenous.

## When the theorem is useful

Partialling out clarifies what a multiple-regression coefficient measures. It
also helps with several applied tasks:

- diagnosing which observations and sources of variation identify a
  coefficient;
- checking that two implementations use the same controls and sample; and
- motivating flexible nuisance-function methods that residualize outcomes and
  treatments before estimating a target effect.

The theorem does not permit controls to be selected without regard to the
research design. Bad controls, measurement error, and omitted confounders
remain bad controls, measurement error, and omitted confounders after
residualization.
